key_insight: Routine health records contained measurable signal that could separate higher- and lower-risk groups after paracetamol overdose, but not with enough accuracy for individual-level clinical decision-making.
clinical_relevance: This suggests risk prediction in self-harm should not be dismissed as impossible, while still not supporting clinical deployment for deciding treatment or suicide risk.
method: 4,095 adults with paracetamol overdose at NHS Lothian EDs (2017–2023)
37 routinely collected EHR features used in elastic-net logistic regression
Predicted death or mental health inpatient admission across 0–7, 8–30, and 31–365 days; 20% held-out test set with bootstrapping
evidence_signal: Bootstrap AUROC confidence intervals were above 0.5 in all time windows (0.65–0.82, 0.63–0.90, 0.71–0.85), and calibration slopes were close to 1.
watch_item: Performance was below what would be needed for safe individual patient use, and the outcome was largely driven by mental health admission rather than death.
paper_title: Reconsidering the case against risk prediction in self-harm: routinely collected health data distinguishes groups at higher and lower risk of adverse outcomes following paracetamol overdose
